summary: From their capital Hattusa in central Anatolia, the Hittite kings Hattusili I and Mursili I raided as far as Aleppo and Babylon (c. 1595 BCE) before the Old Kingdom sank into court strife. Suppiluliuma I (c. 1350–1322 BCE) broke Mitanni and made the Hittites masters of Syria; his successors fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh and made peace. Around 1190 BCE, amid the wider Bronze Age collapse, Hattusa was abandoned and the empire vanished. All dates are approximate (middle chronology).
details: The Hittites, speakers of an Indo-European language, had formed small kingdoms in central Anatolia around Kussara and Kanesh. Around 1650 BCE (middle chronology), Hattusili I, who may also have used the name Labarna, moved the capital from Nesha (Kanesh) to Hattusa, inside the great bend of the Kizilirmak (Halys) river, and took his throne name from it. His annals describe campaigns against Arzawa in the west and into northern Syria, where he attacked but did not take Aleppo, and a crossing of the Euphrates. Central Anatolia became the core of a kingdom that would last over four centuries.

Hattusili's grandson and chosen heir, Mursili I, renewed the wars in Syria. He destroyed Aleppo, capital of the kingdom of Yamhad, which had resisted his grandfather, then led an unprecedented march of some 2,000 kilometres down the Euphrates and sacked Babylon around 1595 BCE, ending Hammurabi's dynasty. Babylonia was far too distant to hold and passed to the Kassites. Back home, Mursili was murdered by his brother-in-law Hantili. Decades of royal murders followed, the Hurrians seized Aleppo and the south-eastern coast, and the Hittite realm shrank back towards central Anatolia.

By the time Telipinu took the throne (c. 1525 BCE), murders and coups had shaken the royal family, and the kingdom had lost its conquests to Arzawa in the west, Mitanni in the east, the Kaska in the north and Kizzuwatna in the south. Telipinu won back some ground by allying with Kizzuwatna. He is best known for the Edict of Telipinu, which set out who should inherit the throne (first-rank sons, then lesser sons, then the husband of a first-rank daughter) to end the bloodshed. After him the Hittites entered a poorly recorded 'Middle Kingdom' of about seventy years.

After a long period of weakness and invasion, the Hittites recovered under Suppiluliuma I (c. 1350–1322 BCE), a successful general who seized the throne after supporters murdered the young heir Tudhaliya. His great rival was Mitanni, the Hurrian kingdom of northern Mesopotamia. In the so-called One-Year War he overran Mitanni's vassals, captured and plundered its capital Washukanni, and crossed into Syria, taking Aleppo, Alalakh, Qatna and other small kingdoms, while Ugarit became his ally. Mitanni was broken, and the map's Hittite realm now spread from Anatolia deep into northern Syria.

The last Mitannian stronghold west of the Euphrates was Carchemish. While besieging it, Suppiluliuma received an astonishing letter from Egypt's widowed queen, most likely Tutankhamun's widow Ankhesenamun: she had no son and asked for one of his sons to marry, so that he would become king of Egypt. After some hesitation he sent his son Zannanza, who was killed on the way. Carchemish fell, and Suppiluliuma made his sons viceroys at Carchemish and Aleppo to rule Hittite Syria. Blaming Egypt for Zannanza's death, he attacked Egyptian territory, opening a long period of hostility.

Suppiluliuma's revenge raids into Egyptian territory brought back prisoners of war, and according to the 'Plague Prayers' of his son Mursili II, those prisoners carried an epidemic into Hatti. People went on dying for at least two decades; some historians suggest the disease was tularaemia. It is often considered the cause of Suppiluliuma's death c. 1322 BCE and of his eldest son and successor, Arnuwanda II, soon afterwards. Mursili II inherited a strong position in Syria but a stricken homeland, and blamed the gods' anger on his father's broken oaths.

Egypt's new 19th Dynasty wanted to win back Syria, and Ramesses II invaded Amurru, a borderland both powers claimed. In May 1274 BCE (by the usual chronology), the Hittite king Muwatalli II ambushed the Egyptian army near Kadesh on the Orontes, after sending spies to mislead Ramesses. Some 5,000–6,000 chariots may have taken part, probably the largest chariot battle ever fought. Ramesses rallied his troops and reinforcements drove off the Hittites, but the battle ended in stalemate. Ramesses withdrew, while Muwatalli went on to seize the Egyptian province of Upi around Damascus, keeping Syria Hittite.

After Muwatalli's death, his son Urhi-Teshub (Mursili III) was overthrown by his uncle Hattusili III, who wanted foreign recognition, while Assyria was seizing the former lands of Mitanni and threatening both empires. Around 1259 BCE, in Ramesses II's 21st year, the two powers agreed the 'Eternal Treaty', the oldest known surviving peace treaty, preserved in both an Egyptian version and Akkadian tablets from Hattusa. Each side promised not to invade the other, to help against attackers or rebels, and to return political refugees. A Hittite princess later married Ramesses, and the Syrian frontier stayed fixed.

Hattusili's son Tudhaliya IV lost ground to Assyria, which defeated him at Nihriya, though he briefly took Cyprus. Around 1207 BCE his younger son Suppiluliuma II succeeded his brother Arnuwanda III amid signs of disloyalty at court. He fought to restore control of southern Anatolia, crushing the rebel city of Tarhuntassa, and his fleet won the first recorded naval battle in history off Cyprus. But urgent grain shipments from Egypt point to famine, and enemies were advancing along the coasts from the west. He is the last Great King of Hatti known for certain.

Around 1190 BCE, as the Late Bronze Age collapse swept the eastern Mediterranean, the Hittite capital came to an end. Excavations suggest Hattusa was gradually abandoned over several decades, possibly amid regional drought; the court may have moved elsewhere, and fire destroyed what remained only after the elites had left. Suppiluliuma II's fate is unknown, and no Hittite king ever returned. The empire vanished as a state and disappears from the map. Only an offshoot survived at Carchemish, whose ruler Kuzi-Teshub, a descendant of Suppiluliuma I, later claimed the title 'Great King'.

Ugarit, a wealthy port on the Syrian coast, had been a Hittite vassal since the days of Suppiluliuma I, trading with Egypt, Cyprus and the Aegean and shipping grain around the region. Its last king, Ammurapi, sent his troops to help the Hittites and his ships to Lukka in Anatolia, leaving his own kingdom exposed. In a famous letter he described enemy ships arriving and his cities burned. Around 1185 BCE Ugarit was destroyed, one of many cities lost in the Late Bronze Age collapse, and with it the Hittites lost their last great ally on the Mediterranean coast.
